Bellman in matrix form

With $n$ states there are $n$ Bellman equations. Stack them and they become one matrix equation, $v = r + \gamma P v$, solved in one line with a matrix inverse. The inverse has a meaning of its own: it counts discounted future visits.

Lesson 16's three-state weather, with a reward for each kind of day (Lesson 27 had two states). Each row of sliders sets where a state goes tomorrow (rows are rescaled to add up to 1). The last column is the reward for a day in that state.

from \ to☀️☁️🌧️$r$

Where the inverse comes from

Add up $\gamma^k P^k$, the discounted chance of being in each state $k$ days from now. Drag $K$ to add more terms and watch the sum approach the inverse above.

The maths

Write the values as a column vector $v$, the expected rewards as $r$ (with $r_i = \mathbb{E}[R_{t+1} \mid S_t = i]$), and the transition probabilities as a matrix $P$ with $P_{ij} = \Pr\{S_{t+1} = j \mid S_t = i\}$. Then all $n$ Bellman equations at once read

$$v = r + \gamma P v$$

Row $i$ of $Pv$ is $\sum_j P_{ij} v_j$, the expected next value from state $i$, so this is exactly Lesson 27's pair of equations, for any number of states. Collect the $v$ terms:

$$(I - \gamma P)\, v = r \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = (I - \gamma P)^{-1} r$$

The inverse exists whenever $\gamma < 1$. Expanding it as a geometric series of matrices shows why:

$$(I - \gamma P)^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k P^k$$

$P^k_{ij}$ is the probability of being in $j$ exactly $k$ steps after starting in $i$. Every row of $P^k$ sums to 1, so the terms shrink like $\gamma^k$ and the series converges. Multiplying by $I - \gamma P$ telescopes it to $I$.

So entry $(i, j)$ of the inverse is the expected discounted number of visits to $j$ when starting from $i$. Each row sums to $\sum_k \gamma^k = 1/(1 - \gamma)$. Then $v_i = \sum_j (\text{discounted visits to } j) \times r_j$: rewards weighted by how much time you spend collecting them.

The catch is cost. Inverting an $n \times n$ matrix takes about $n^3$ operations. That is nothing for 3 states, slow for a million, and impossible for the roughly $10^{170}$ positions of Go. That is why the rest of the course uses iterative methods (Lesson 30) and sampling.
